topic.title_target: Il presente e gli usi di base di avere
topic.title_en: Present forms and basic uses of avere
learning_objectives: Recognise and produce all six present indicative forms of avere.
Use avere for simple possession and family relationships.
Express age with avere + number + anni.
Use checked A1 expressions such as avere fame, sete, freddo, caldo and paura.

skills.description_en: Recognise and produce the six present indicative forms of avere.
Use avere to say that a person has or possesses a person, animal or thing.
Express age with avere + number + anni.
Use checked beginner expressions with avere, including fame, sete, freddo, caldo and paura.
Choose the correct form and basic meaning of avere from a short context.
Produce short natural A1 sentences with avere for possession, age and common physical or emotional states.

lesson.short_explanation_en: Avere means “to have”, but at A1 it does more than express possession. Its present forms are ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete and hanno. Use avere for things or relationships (Ho un fratello), for age (Ho diciotto anni), and in common expressions such as avere fame, sete, freddo, caldo and paura. Italian normally omits a clear subject pronoun, so Ho un libro is more neutral than Io ho un libro unless io is contrastive.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Avere is irregular in the present. The six forms must be learned individually. The initial h in ho, hai, ha and hanno is written but not pronounced.
rule_blocks.pattern: ho · hai · ha · abbiamo · avete · hanno
usage_notes_en: Match the verb form to the grammatical subject.
As with other Italian verbs, omit a clear subject pronoun unless it is useful for contrast or clarity.
common_errors_en: Incorrect: Io ha un libro. Correct: Ho un libro.
Incorrect: Marco ho una macchina. Correct: Marco ha una macchina.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Use avere + noun phrase to say that someone has a thing, animal or family relationship.
usage_notes_en: Ho un libro means I have a book.
Ho un fratello is the normal way to say that you have a brother.
common_errors_en: Do not replace avere with essere when the meaning is possession.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Italian states age with avere, followed by a number and anni. English uses “be”, so this pattern needs to be learned as an Italian construction.
usage_notes_en: Ho diciotto anni = I am eighteen years old.
For one third-person subject: Marco ha diciannove anni.
common_errors_en: Incorrect: Sono diciotto anni. Correct: Ho diciotto anni.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Several frequent physical and emotional states use avere in Italian. This lesson practises only checked A1 expressions.
rule_blocks.pattern: avere + fame / sete / freddo / caldo / paura
usage_notes_en: Ho fame = I am hungry; ho sete = I am thirsty.
Ha freddo = he/she is cold; ha caldo = he/she is warm/hot.
common_errors_en: Incorrect for the physical sensation: Anna è freddo. Correct: Anna ha freddo.

contexts.setting_en: Two young people introduce themselves and mention their age and family.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.target: Ciao, sono Anna. Ho diciotto anni. Ho un fratello.
lines.translation_en: Hi, I’m Anna. I’m eighteen years old. I have a brother.

lines.speaker: Marco
lines.target: Ciao, sono Marco. Ho diciannove anni. Ho una sorella.
lines.translation_en: Hi, I’m Marco. I’m nineteen years old. I have a sister.

focus_items.explanation_en: Italian expresses age with avere: ho diciotto anni.
The same present form expresses possession or family relationships.
Marco also uses first-person singular ho for his age.
Io is explicit here for contrast, but the verb form remains ho.
The first-person singular form is ho.

contexts.setting_en: A short description of how members of a family feel at home.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.target: Anna ha fame e Marco ha sete.
lines.translation_en: Anna is hungry and Marco is thirsty.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.target: La mamma ha freddo. Il papà ha caldo.
lines.translation_en: Mum is cold. Dad is warm.

focus_items.explanation_en: Avere fame is the standard beginner expression for being hungry.
Avere sete is used for being thirsty.
Avere freddo uses avere, not essere.
Avere caldo uses avere, not essere.
Avere paura is used to express fear.

examples.note_en: Ho is first-person singular; Italian normally omits io when it is clear.
Hai is the second-person singular present form.
A named singular person takes ha.
Abbiamo is the first-person plural form.
Avete is the second-person plural form.

examples.target: Anna e Marco hanno un cane.
examples.translation_en: Anna and Marco have a dog.
examples.note_en: A plural third-person subject takes hanno.
Italian uses avere, literally “to have years”, to state age.
Use ha + number + anni for one third-person subject.
Fame and sete are common nouns used with avere.

examples.target: Anna ha freddo e Marco ha caldo.
examples.translation_en: Anna is cold and Marco is warm.
examples.note_en: Italian uses avere for these physical sensations.
